title: US Tourist Praises Mumbai Locals After Free Treatment at Government Hospital
excerpt: An American visitor who twisted his ankle in Mumbai was helped by locals and received free X-ray and treatment at a government hospital, drawing sharp comparisons with US healthcare costs.
body:
• A US tourist in Mumbai twisted his ankle and was helped by locals who took him to a nearby government hospital for free treatment.
  • The hospital provided an X-ray, examination, and ankle wrap at no cost, leaving the tourist stunned by the contrast with US healthcare pricing.
  • The viral Instagram video, shared on August 24 by India First Post, has reignited debate about the gap between Indian and American healthcare costs.
  • Similar treatment in a US emergency room can run into thousands of dollars, even with insurance coverage.

An American tourist travelling through Mumbai got an unexpected lesson in Indian hospitality and public healthcare after twisting his ankle — and walking away from a government hospital without paying a single rupee.

The incident, captured on video and shared on Instagram on August 24 by the account India First Post, shows the tourist sitting in visible pain after injuring his ankle. When he told bystanders he had no money for medical treatment, several locals stepped in to reassure him.

"You don't have to pay any money. Okay, it's a government hospital."

— A Mumbai local, speaking to the injured tourist

Strangers Step In

The video shows multiple locals helping the injured man to his feet and guiding him toward a nearby government hospital. "Wait, I'll hold you," one person can be heard saying as they supported the tourist during the walk.

The response was immediate and matter-of-fact — no hesitation, no negotiation. For the bystanders, directing a stranger to a free public hospital was routine. For the American visitor, it was anything but.

"Very, very nice locals helping a foreigner again as always. So yeah, amazing Indians," the tourist said as he made his way to the facility.

Free X-Ray, Treatment, and Wrap

At the government hospital, the tourist underwent an X-ray, received treatment for his ankle injury, and was given a wrap to support the joint — all without being asked to pay.

"That is incredible, the fact that they took me in, didn't charge me, X-rayed me, gave me a wrap and did it all without taking any of my money," he said after leaving the hospital.

The experience prompted a blunt comparison with the US healthcare system. "So absolutely incredible service from the government hospital here in Mumbai. You will not find that back home in the US," he said. "We have a horrible medical system where they will take thousands of dollars for this kind of treatment."

India vs. US: The Cost Gap

The tourist's reaction echoes a familiar refrain among Americans who encounter Indian public healthcare. In the United States, a basic emergency room visit for a similar injury — examination, X-ray, and bandaging — can easily exceed $2,000 before insurance, according to multiple reports.

Earlier this year, an Indian man shared his $6,354 hospital bill for a 90-minute US emergency room visit after injuring his knee while ice skating. Doctors examined him, took an X-ray, and wrapped a crepe bandage around the injury. Even with insurance, he paid $1,800 out of pocket, according to Inshorts.

India's network of government-run hospitals provides free or heavily subsidised care across the country. While these facilities often face criticism for overcrowding and resource constraints, the basic access they offer — particularly for emergency treatment — remains a sharp contrast to the cost barriers many Americans face.

A Pattern of Viral Healthcare Stories

The Mumbai video is the latest in a string of viral clips featuring foreign visitors expressing surprise at India's low healthcare costs. In June, a separate video of a US tourist receiving a free rabies vaccine at an Indian government hospital was widely shared, drawing attention from political figures and sparking similar online discussions.

In September 2025, American expat Kristen Fischer went viral after sharing that she paid just ₹50 — roughly 60 US cents — for treatment of a thumb injury at a local hospital, comparing it to monthly US insurance premiums of $1,000 to $2,000.

What It Means for the Diaspora

For Indian Americans and NRIs, these stories underscore a reality many already know: routine medical care in India costs a fraction of what it does in the United States. The growing visibility of these comparisons on social media has fed broader conversations about medical tourism, healthcare reform in the US, and the often-overlooked strengths of India's public health infrastructure.

The Hindustan Times, which reported on the Mumbai ankle incident, noted that the video is based on user-generated social media content and has not been independently verified.
nri_angle: The viral video highlights the stark cost gap between Indian public healthcare and the US system, a reality familiar to many NRIs who navigate both.
author: Diaspora Desk
